analysis.one_liner: Exempts companies selling scrap paper, metal, and batteries for recycling from toxic cleanup liability.
analysis.headline: A bill to shield scrap and battery sellers from Superfund cleanup lawsuits gathered 64 Senate cosponsors and the sponsorship of both party leaders, but the environment committee never voted on it and it died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Superfund law so that companies that sell or send scrap paper, plastic, glass, textiles, rubber, metal, or used batteries for recycling could no longer be forced to pay for cleaning up pollution at the recycling facilities that received the material. Sellers would qualify if the scrap met commercial market standards and a real market existed for it, and — for deals struck more than 90 days after enactment — if they took reasonable care to check that the receiving facility obeyed environmental laws. Supporters said Superfund liability had unintentionally scared companies away from recycling; the bill never received a committee vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that generate or trade recyclable scrap — paper mills, steel and aluminum producers, scrap metal dealers, and lead-acid and nickel-cadmium battery makers — would no longer face lawsuits making them share cleanup costs when a recycler they sold to contaminated a site. Recycling processors themselves would also be relieved of the threat of contribution suits, and the bill would penalize anyone who sued a protected party by making them pay that party's legal and expert-witness fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Scrap metal, paper, and battery companies

how_it_helps.text: Exempts anyone who arranged a recycling transaction from Superfund arranger liability — the part of the law that makes companies that sent waste to a site help pay for its cleanup — for the covered scrap materials.

Covers scrap paper, plastic, glass, textiles, rubber (except whole tires), scrap metal, and spent lead-acid, nickel-cadmium, and other batteries, treating sales of these as recycling if the material met a commercial specification grade and a market existed for it.

States the purpose plainly: to remove 'disincentives and impediments to recycling created as an unintended consequence of the 1980 Superfund liability provisions' and to put recycled materials on equal legal footing with virgin raw materials.
Deters future cleanup suits against protected recyclers by making anyone who sues them anyway pay their full defense costs, including attorney and expert witness fees.
For battery transactions, the shield applies to any seller who complied with applicable federal battery recycling regulations — a lighter test than proving the receiving site was clean.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the Superfund trust fund, and the people who live near contaminated recycling sites. When a recycling facility turns out to be a pollution source, cleanup costs that once could be recovered from the companies that sent material there would instead fall to the public fund — or the site would simply go uncleaned if the fund did not cover it. Neighboring communities would lose their main lever for making generators pay for lead, cadmium, or solvent contamination traced back to scrap they sold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people near contaminated recycling sites

drawbacks.text: The core effect is a cost shift: liability that today can be spread across the companies that arranged for material to be recycled would move to the Superfund trust fund and to any remaining liable parties, so the public backstops cleanups at recycling sites.

The safeguards lean heavily on the seller's own judgment. The 'reasonable care' check on the receiving facility only applies to transactions 90 or more days after enactment, and the exemption survives unless the seller had an objectively reasonable basis to know the material would not be recycled or the facility was violating the law — a standard set by factors like the seller's business size and industry custom.

The material-based carve-outs are narrow: scrap stays protected unless it held PCBs above 50 parts per million or, for scrap paper, a hazard level EPA formally determined to be a significant risk — contamination at the receiving site from other substances would still be shielded.

The bill does not affect already-concluded or already-pending government cleanup actions, so it offers relief only going forward — meaning companies get future immunity while past liabilities the public already absorbed stay absorbed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targeted was real: fear of open-ended Superfund liability genuinely deterred companies from selling scrap for recycling, which is an environmental loss. But the remedy was one-sided. It did not condition the exemption on the receiving facility being clean — only on the seller having acted with reasonable care by its own industry's standards — and it stripped communities of the polluter-pays lever that made generators answer for where their scrap ended up. A narrower bill, or one pairing the exemption with a dedicated cleanup fund for recycling sites, would have balanced the tradeoff better; this version largely moved the risk from well-capitalized scrap generators to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never took the bill up, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott introduced the bill on June 16, 1998 together with Minority Leader Tom Daschle — an unusual show of bipartisan leadership sponsorship for a liability bill.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day; it never left that committee.
Supporters kept the bill visible by inserting sponsor remarks into the Congressional Record in June, September, and October 1998, but no markup, hearing vote, or floor vote followed.

By October 1998 the bill had 64 cosponsors — 34 Republicans and 30 Democrats, a majority of the Senate — yet the session ended January 3, 1999 without the committee or the full Senate ever voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, companies that send scrap and batteries for recycling remained on the hook to help pay for cleanups when recyclers contaminated sites — so communities near those sites and the Superfund's polluter-pays principle came out ahead for that Congress, while the scrap, paper, and battery industries did not get the liability shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Polluter-pays liability and communities near recycling sites

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly evenly split — 34 Republicans and 30 Democrats cosponsored, and the two party leaders introduced the bill together — but the bill died in committee, so there was never a roll call to measure the split.

industries.note: Scrap dealers and metal producers would be freed from paying for contamination at the recycling facilities that bought their material, as long as the scrap met market specs and they took reasonable care. This removes a real deterrent to recycling but also shifts cleanup risk at those facilities onto the public fund.

industries.industry: Lead-acid and nickel-cadmium battery makers and lead smelters
industries.note: Battery recycling sites handle lead and cadmium and have been major sources of toxic contamination; the bill would exempt any seller who complied with federal battery regulations from helping pay to clean such sites, leaving the cost to the Superfund trust fund and nearby residents.

Industrial generators of scrap paper, plastic, and glass would gain liability relief for materials they send to recyclers, encouraging recycling streams but externalizing the risk that downstream facilities are contaminated.
Cleanup costs that the law currently recovers from companies that arranged recycling transactions would fall to the publicly backed fund when recycling sites need remediation.
